I am fifty years old and I have farmed my whole life in Quzhou County, though I never went to school. My mother taught me everything I know about the land. I have six mu of fields, and every year I do what my neighbors do and what my family has always done. I cannot afford to take big risks because my family depends on this food and this income.

Last autumn I already sowed my winter wheat with improved seeds from the township supply store—the same kind my neighbor Lao Wang plants, because his yields are always steady. Now that spring is here, the wheat is greening up. I will rotary-till the soil once to break up the crust and keep the moisture in. I irrigate three times: once when the wheat wakes up, once when the stems start growing tall, and once when the heads are flowering. I cannot skip the irrigation because the spring winds here dry out the soil fast. For fertilizer, I spread one bag of compound fertilizer per mu before the first irrigation, and then I topdress with urea when the wheat is jointing. I spray for insects twice, herbicide once, and fungicide once because two years ago the rust came late and wiped out half my grain, and I will not let that happen again. I expect about 500 kilograms of wheat per mu if the weather holds.

After we harvest the wheat in early June, I will plant hybrid maize—Nongda 372, the same variety as last year—directly into the wheat stubble without tilling. No-tillage saves me diesel money and time, and the extension man said it keeps the soil from drying out. Maize needs two irrigations, one when it is knee-high and one when the tassels come out. I spray for corn borers twice and herbicide once. I do not bother with fungicide on maize because in my experience it does fine without it. I hope for 550 kilograms per mu, though if the summer rains are good it might be more.

This is my plan because it is what works. Everyone in my village plants wheat and maize in rotation. If I planted only one crop and it failed, my family would go hungry. Two crops are my insurance. I do not try fancy new methods because I cannot afford to fail. I watch what the good farmers around me do, and I copy them.
